papers.title: The role of social media influencers in nation branding and relationship building with foreign audiences
papers.authors: Hyun Ju Park and Joon Soo Lim
papers.category: 甲亢哥访华 · adjacent nation-branding mechanism
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative repository record verified
papers.takeaway: This study examines how social media influencers negotiate identity and communication strategy when addressing foreign audiences for nation-branding and public-diplomacy purposes. Its findings emphasize that cultural-exchange content is more effective than one-sided host-country promotion, that shared and different cultural backgrounds shape reception, and that disrespect toward an audience's culture produces negative reactions. The article does not study IShowSpeed, but it directly addresses the broader mechanism linking influencer communication to relationship building with foreign publics.

papers.title: Short-form travel vlogs: The influence of parasocial interaction on viewers’ destination–self congruence and behavioural intention
papers.authors: Made Handijaya Dewantara, Xin Jin, and Sarah Gardiner
papers.category: 甲亢哥访华 · adjacent travel-vlog mechanism
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative repository record verified
papers.takeaway: Australian Millennials (N = 459) watched a short-form travel vlog and completed an online survey. Vlogger attractiveness, attitude homophily, and perceived technology skill predicted parasocial interaction, which in turn predicted viewer-destination self-congruence, travel intention, and willingness to generate electronic word of mouth. Vlogger credibility had a negative but nonsignificant association with parasocial interaction. This is adjacent travel-vlog mechanism evidence rather than an IShowSpeed or China-image study.

papers.title: From breach to fulfilment: navigating digital natives’ AI-induced psychological contracts for workplace outcomes
papers.category: Workplace AI and well-being · direct evidence
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative repository record verified
papers.takeaway: A survey of 415 digital-native employees in Indian high-technology industries examines psychological contracts formed with generative AI. Experiences of bias, privacy breach, and opacity are treated as contract breach and are associated with worse innovative-work and well-being outcomes. Perceived contract fulfilment buffers the negative association only when breach is relatively low. The cross-sectional self-report design cannot establish causal effects, but it directly links workplace GenAI experiences to employee well-being.

papers.title: Relying on AI at work reduces self-efficacy, ownership, and meaning while active collaboration mitigates the effects
papers.category: Workplace AI and well-being · direct experimental evidence
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative repository record verified
papers.takeaway: Across workplace-task experiments, passive reliance on AI lowered self-efficacy, psychological ownership, and perceived meaning in work. Passive use could initially raise enjoyment and satisfaction, but these benefits reversed after participants returned to manual work. More active human-AI collaboration mitigated the losses, indicating that the design of AI involvement, rather than AI access alone, shapes worker experience. The experiments focus on proximal psychological outcomes rather than long-term organizational well-being.

papers.title: Working with Generative AI vs Humans: The Impact on Well-being
papers.authors: Eirini Spiliotopoulou, Tim Kraft, Shawn Mankad, and Yanchong Zheng
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative repository record verified
papers.takeaway: An incentivized laboratory experiment assigns participants to complete two operational tasks with either a GenAI assistant or a human collaborator. Validated psychological scales and text analyses indicate lower mental well-being in human-GenAI collaboration than in human-human collaboration. Human pairs reduced negative emotions, whereas human-GenAI pairs did not; human-GenAI collaboration reduced positive emotions, whereas human-human collaboration did not. Transcript analyses associate human interaction with more expressive and uncertainty language and AI interaction with more technical, task-oriented communication. This working paper has not completed journal peer review.

toc.title: Artificially alive: An exploration of AI resurrections and spectral labor modes in a postmortal society
toc.abstractEn: A comparative analysis of 50 AI-resurrection cases identifies spectacular, sociopolitical, and everyday modes and theorizes the extraction of data, likeness, and affect from the dead as spectral labor.

toc.title: Misreading uncivil and intolerant anti-immigration content in digital spheres: The role of recent online perpetration
toc.abstractEn: The study examines how people distinguish incivility from intolerance in anti-immigration content and how recent participation in online hostility shapes those judgments.

toc.title: Parasitic activism: Grassroots electronics repair in and against big tech
toc.abstractEn: This article analyzes grassroots electronics repair as activism that both depends on and contests the infrastructures and restrictions of large technology firms.

toc.title: Young women’s perceptions of cooperative privacy threats through the lens of abortion in the United States
toc.abstractEn: Using abortion as a critical case, the study investigates how young women understand privacy risks created jointly by institutions, platforms, and people in their social networks.

toc.title: AI generation of rage bait: Implications for digital harms
toc.abstractEn: Digital-ethnographic cases show how generative AI can industrialize rage bait and intensify abusive engagement, linking automated content production to platform incentives and digital harm.

toc.title: Cruel companionship: How AI companions exploit loneliness and commodify intimacy
toc.abstractEn: A political-economy and cultural-studies analysis develops cruel companionship to explain how AI products promise intimacy while monetizing attachment and reproducing racialized and gendered hierarchies.

toc.title: The journalists’ exodus: Navigating the transition from Twitter to Mastodon and other alternative platforms
toc.abstractEn: Computational traces from 861 journalists and qualitative evidence examine how journalists navigated platform migration after Twitter’s ownership change and why alternative platforms struggled to replace established networks.

toc.title: ‘I just go headbutt a tree or something’: Children’s contextualised digital play drivers and subjective well-being in the United Kingdom, South Africa, Australia and Cyprus
toc.abstractEn: Cross-national qualitative research situates children’s digital play and subjective well-being within family, material, cultural, and environmental contexts rather than treating screen time as a uniform exposure.

toc.title: Affective liquidity, synthetic bonds: VTubers as posthuman mediators of digital intimacies
toc.abstractEn: A nine-month digital ethnography and 21 fan interviews show how VTubers combine human performance and digital artifice to produce flexible but meaningful forms of mediated intimacy.

toc.title: Dead formats, living futures: Speculative nostalgia and the MiniDisc
toc.abstractEn: The article uses the contemporary revival of MiniDisc to theorize speculative nostalgia as engagement with unrealized technological futures rather than simple restoration of the past.

toc.title: Examining how search engine users understand the production of Autocomplete suggestions
toc.abstractEn: The research maps ordinary users’ folk theories of how autocomplete suggestions are produced and considers how those beliefs affect interpretation of algorithmic outputs.

toc.title: How social responses to online hate messages affect hatefulness
toc.abstractEn: Sequential analyses of one thousand hateful posts test whether social feedback and subsequent interaction amplify or constrain the toxicity of later posts by the same users.

toc.title: Negotiating extremism: Thematic engagement capacity for red pill conversations on Reddit
toc.abstractEn: A topic-network and content analysis of r/PurplePillDebate examines which themes sustain engagement between supporters and critics of red-pill ideology and where deliberation breaks down.

toc.title: Shade visibility: Assessing the algorithmic role of colorism in the perception of Black beauty influencers
toc.abstractEn: The study investigates how platform visibility and skin-tone bias shape perceptions of Black beauty influencers, placing colorism within algorithmic and audience evaluation processes.

toc.title: Engineering epistemic churn: A theory of prolonged meaning-making under platform conditions
toc.abstractEn: The article theorizes epistemic churn as platform-driven cycles of unresolved interpretation that keep publics engaged without producing convergence or stable meaning.

toc.title: Is “Good vibes only” really good? Investigating perceptions of toxic positivity on social media
toc.abstractEn: The study tests when positive social-media messages are perceived as toxic positivity and how such perceptions qualify simple emotional-contagion expectations.

toc.title: Racial-ethnic differences in adolescents’ daily enactment of critical race digital literacy skills: A daily diary study
toc.abstractEn: A daily-diary design examines how adolescents from different racial and ethnic groups enact critical race digital-literacy practices in everyday social-media use.

toc.title: The block log: 20 years of content moderation on Wikipedia
toc.abstractEn: Two decades of English Wikipedia blocking records reveal how a volunteer platform adapted moderation as visibility increased and participation declined.

toc.title: When AI fact-checks false short-form health videos: Effects of AI-driven fact-checking on credibility assessment of the videos
toc.abstractEn: Experiments compare AI and human fact-checking cues on false short-form health videos to assess how source attribution changes credibility judgments.

toc.title: “I am Neuro, who are you?”: Performances of authenticity in an experimental AI livestream
toc.abstractEn: The article examines how an experimental AI livestream performs authenticity and how audiences negotiate the appeal and anxiety of apparently humanlike AI interaction.

toc.title: A strong digital society with digitally skilled people: The discursive construction of digital exclusion and inclusion in newspaper media
toc.abstractEn: Critical discourse analysis of Flemish newspapers shows how digital inclusion and exclusion are constructed amid major public investment in digitalization.

toc.title: Journalism and social media in creator economies: Evolving structures and labor
toc.abstractEn: The study analyzes how legacy journalism and social-media creator economies converge, reshaping organizational structures, labor conditions, and professional boundaries.

toc.title: Close to you: How location cue affects responses to self-disclosures on social media
toc.abstractEn: Research on visible user-location labels tests how geographic cues alter responses to self-disclosure on social media, including perceptions of closeness and social evaluation.

toc.title: Feminist television, racist Twitter? Feminist perspectives on the mediation of sexual misconduct in the Netherlands
toc.abstractEn: The article compares public television and Twitter in the mediation of sexual misconduct in the Netherlands and uses feminist theory to identify tensions between gender justice and racialized discourse.

toc.title: Revising a measure of anti-oppressive social media literacy through the use of cognitive interviewing
toc.abstractEn: Cognitive interviews are used to revise a measure of anti-oppressive social-media literacy so that it captures politically situated recognition, reflection, and action.

toc.title: ‘My Europe Builds Walls’: A cross-platform visual analysis of the Sweden Democrats’ 2024 EU election campaign
toc.abstractEn: A qualitatively centered cross-platform analysis examines visual securitization in the Sweden Democrats’ 2024 European Parliament campaign.

toc.title: The Tate-space on YouTube: Ambient ideology and the limits of platform moderation
toc.abstractEn: Two empirical analyses trace how Andrew Tate-related content persisted and transformed on YouTube after official-channel removal, exposing limits of channel-level moderation.

toc.title: Aspiring toward decency: Collectively and creatively appropriating information communication technology in Havana
toc.abstractEn: Interviews and ethnography in Havana examine resolver as collective, creative appropriation of communication technology under persistent scarcity.

toc.title: From hits to unicorns: Venture capital in the videogame industry
toc.abstractEn: Investment data and industry discourse are analyzed to explain how venture capital financializes videogame production and reorients expectations from hit products to scalable firms.

toc.title: Reaching a larger audience: Content-related strategies of the far right on VK
toc.abstractEn: The article identifies content strategies used by far-right actors on VK to expand audience reach and normalize ideology beyond commonly studied Western platforms.

toc.title: “A safe, responsible, and profitable ecosystem of music”: Analyzing perceptions and implementation of generative AI in the music industry
toc.abstractEn: Ethnographic fieldwork at music-industry conferences analyzes competing understandings of generative AI and how responsibility claims are translated into commercial practice.

toc.title: Beyond textual disinformation: Comparing the effects of textual disinformation to AI-generated and video-based visual disinformation across different issues
toc.abstractEn: Comparative experiments test whether textual, conventional visual, and AI-generated visual disinformation produce different effects across political issues.

toc.title: Screenshots in human communication research: Protecting privacy in light of law, ethics and user expectations
toc.abstractEn: The article evaluates screenshots as research data and offers privacy guidance grounded in legal obligations, research ethics, and users’ contextual expectations.

papers.title: A twelve-language dataset for the study of event descriptions in expository and narrative texts

papers.category: 综合顶刊 · social-science data descriptor
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative repository record verified
papers.takeaway: This Data Descriptor reports a standardized online text-elicitation study with 1,200 participants, 100 in each of 12 language groups. Every participant described two events in both expository and narrative genres, producing 2,400 short texts. The dataset supports comparisons of how writers, languages, and genres shape descriptions of the same events and includes participant demographics and reusable experimental materials. It is relevant to social-science and cross-cultural communication research as an openly available multilingual data resource.

papers.title: Genre-convention congruence and narrative immersion: The mediating roles of emotional engagement and character identification in viewers' sharing intentions
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative repository record verified
papers.takeaway: This two-study article examines perceived genre-convention congruence, narrative immersion, emotional engagement, character identification, and sharing intentions around the Korean drama Queen of Tears. A survey of 377 Chinese adults who had watched all 16 episodes found positive associations linking perceived congruence to immersion, immersion to emotional engagement and identification, and those responses to sharing intentions. In a clip experiment with 88 retained participants, only immersion remained significant after Holm correction; the clips also differed in plot and character circumstances. The evidence is therefore adjacent, reverse-direction cross-cultural reception evidence rather than a study of foreign reception of Chinese mythology.

papers.title: The dimensionality and cross-cultural invariance of narrative transportability: evidence from 50 countries and 21 languages
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative repository record verified
papers.takeaway: Using 8,814 participants from 50 countries and 21 languages, this study evaluates the dimensionality and cross-cultural measurement invariance of narrative transportability. Exploratory analysis on 2,644 participants identifies cognitive involvement, cognitive-emotional imagination, sensory imagination, and personal involvement as four dimensions, followed by confirmatory and cross-cultural tests in the remaining sample. The article supplies measurement evidence for comparing narrative receptivity across cultures, but it does not test Chinese mythology, value congruence, or character-level reception directly.
